prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- Rapes targeting girls as young as seven are on the increase in Afghanistan where conditions for women are little better than under the Taliban, the U.N. and rights groups say. Conditions for women are little better than they were under the hardline Taliban regime, the U.N. says. In its annual report on human rights, the U.N. warned conditions were deteriorating in the war-ravaged country despite U.S.-led efforts after the 2001 removal from power of the hardline militia. "Violence is tolerated or condoned within the family and community, within traditional and religious leadership circles, as well as the formal and informal justice system," said Navi Pillay, the U.N. high commissioner for human rights. The "Afghan government has failed to adequately protect the rights of women despite constitutional guarantees." With a resurgent Taliban targeting NATO forces, government security forces and civilians, violence has been on the increase in Afghanistan.. The number of civilian casualties in 2008 totaled 2,118 -- the highest number recorded since the ouster of the Taliban in 2001, the U.N. said, urging greater protecting for ordinary Afghans. Violence against women comes in the form of rape, "honor killings," early and forced marriages, sexual abuse and slavery, the report says. "The security is the big issue," said Suraya Pakzad, founder of the Voice of Women Organization, which promotes education and awareness of women's rights and protects women and girls at risk in Afghanistan. "Because of security we, unfortunately, day by day, we have to pull out of areas where last year we operated, we have our operations. We were able to work with the women, but this year we cannot," she said. "We have to leave the area because security is getting worse day by day." "Rapes in the country have been growing tremendously, particularly child rapes within the ages of 9, 8, 7, even lesser than that," said Wazhma Frogh, director of Global Rights Afghanistan. "So these are the issues that are all born by this lack of security where women have no place in ... security decisions." Domestic violence against child brides is widespread, said Suraya Pakzad, the founder of the Voice of Women organization, who was married at age 14 and has six children. She said girls as young as 10 face "violation" by husbands 40 years their senior. "By the end ... women, or girls, run away." But women without husbands, especially widows, may have it even worse in Afghanistan, the report says. Without a spouse, the women are reduced to begging to feed their children. Options outside the home are limited where the Taliban holds sway in Afghanistan. The Taliban's interpretation of strict Islamic law, or sharia, has included banning girls from school and the workplace. Even in areas not overrun by the Taliban, women face risks outside the home. "The assassination of the most prominent national female senior police officer, in Kandahar in September 2008, underscores the tremendous risks faced by women in public life," the report says.

outputs.L2:
**UNITED NATIONS (CNN) —** The United Nations and human rights organizations say rape is rising in Afghanistan, with victims including girls aged seven and possibly younger. They also warn that life for Afghan women has improved little since the Taliban’s rule.

In its yearly human rights assessment, the U.N. said the situation in the conflict-ravaged country was worsening despite U.S.-led initiatives launched after the hardline Taliban movement was removed from power in 2001.

Navi Pillay, the U.N. high commissioner for human rights, said abuse is accepted or permitted by families and communities, traditional and religious leaders, and both official and unofficial judicial institutions. She added that Afghanistan’s government has not sufficiently defended women’s rights, even though those rights are guaranteed by the constitution.

Overall violence has intensified as the revived Taliban attacks NATO troops, Afghan security personnel and civilians. According to the U.N., 2,118 civilians were killed in 2008—the highest annual total documented since the Taliban’s 2001 overthrow. The organization called for stronger protection of ordinary Afghans.

The report said violence against women includes rape, so-called honor killings, sexual exploitation and enslavement, as well as marriages that are forced or take place at an early age.

Suraya Pakzad, who founded the Voice of Women Organization, identified insecurity as the central problem. Her organization works to educate people about women’s rights and to protect vulnerable Afghan women and girls. Pakzad said worsening security has forced the group to withdraw gradually from places where it had operated the previous year. Although staff members had previously been able to assist local women, they could no longer continue working in those areas and had to leave.

Wazhma Frogh, director of Global Rights Afghanistan, said rape had increased dramatically across the country. She noted that many victims were children aged nine, eight or seven, and sometimes even younger. Frogh linked these abuses to the absence of security and to women’s exclusion from decisions concerning it.

Pakzad also said domestic abuse of young brides is common. Married at 14 herself and now the mother of six children, she said girls as young as 10 may be subjected to violations by husbands who are 40 years older. Eventually, she said, some of these women and girls flee.

The U.N. report indicated that women without husbands—particularly widows—can face even harsher circumstances. Many are forced to beg in order to provide food for their children.

In Afghan regions controlled by the Taliban, women have few opportunities beyond the household. Under the movement’s strict interpretation of Islamic law, or sharia, girls have been prohibited from attending school, and women have been barred from working.

Women remain in danger in public even in places not controlled by the Taliban. The report pointed to the September 2008 assassination in Kandahar of the country’s most prominent senior female police officer as evidence of the severe threats confronting women who take public roles.
outputs.L3:
The United Nations reported that conditions for women in Afghanistan continued to deteriorate and remained only marginally better than they had been under Taliban rule. Women and girls faced widespread violence, including rape, honor killings, early and forced marriage, sexual abuse, and slavery. Reports also indicated a disturbing increase in the rape of very young girls.

Despite constitutional guarantees of women’s rights, the Afghan government failed to provide adequate protection or effective access to justice. Violence against women was frequently tolerated—or insufficiently challenged—by families, local communities, religious leaders, and both formal and informal justice systems. At the same time, worsening security and the expanding Taliban insurgency forced women’s rights organizations to withdraw from areas in which they had previously operated, further limiting support for vulnerable women and girls. The broader security situation was equally grave: civilian casualties reached 2,118 in 2008, the highest annual total recorded since the Taliban’s removal from power in 2001.
outputs.L4:
The United Nations and Afghan human rights organizations warned that violence against women and girls was worsening as insecurity spread across Afghanistan. Drawing on an annual human rights report and testimony from local advocates, they described a climate in which victims often had little access to protection, justice, medical care, or safe shelter.

The findings pointed to a sharp increase in reported rapes, including assaults on girls as young as seven. Rights advocates also documented honor killings, forced and underage marriages, domestic abuse, abductions, and other forms of gender-based violence. Because many families fear stigma, retaliation, or punishment for reporting such crimes, campaigners said the documented cases likely represented only a fraction of the true total.

Although the Afghan government had adopted laws and institutions intended to safeguard women, enforcement remained weak and inconsistent. Police and courts frequently failed to investigate complaints, while perpetrators could escape punishment through family influence, informal settlements, or discriminatory local practices. In some cases, women seeking help risked being blamed, detained, or returned to abusive households.

Local advocates argued that deepening conflict and political instability had further undermined the limited gains women had made. In areas where state authority was weak, conservative customs and armed groups restricted women’s movement, education, employment, and access to public life. Activists said these conditions left many Afghan women with protections that existed largely on paper.

Taken together, the report and testimony suggested that the government had not done enough to prevent violence or hold offenders accountable. Rights groups concluded that, for many women and girls, daily life remained marked by fear, coercion, and impunity, leaving their circumstances only marginally better than they had been under Taliban rule.

**The United Nations and CNN in a Connected World**

The **United Nations** plays a central role in addressing international challenges such as conflict, poverty, climate change, human rights, and humanitarian crises. By bringing countries together, the organization provides a forum for diplomacy and global cooperation.

News organizations such as **CNN** help the public follow these issues by reporting from different regions, interviewing officials and experts, and explaining how international decisions affect communities. Coverage of United Nations meetings, peacekeeping missions, and emergency relief efforts can make complex global events more accessible to a broad audience.

Although the United Nations and CNN have distinct roles—one as an international organization and the other as a news network—both influence how people understand global affairs. Reliable institutions, independent journalism, and careful fact-checking remain essential in an increasingly connected world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about the U.N.’s warning that violence against women and girls is increasing in Afghanistan, including statistics and quotes from women’s rights advocates.
counterfactuals.output:
# UN warns violence against women and girls is rising in Afghanistan as Taliban restrictions deepen

**Kabul, Afghanistan —** Violence against women and girls is increasing in Afghanistan, the United Nations has warned, as sweeping Taliban restrictions leave survivors with fewer ways to seek protection, medical care or justice.

UN officials say the dismantling of legal protections, the closure of many women’s shelters and the exclusion of women from large parts of public life have created an environment in which abuse can occur with greater impunity. Women attempting to report violence may be required to bring a male guardian, while some risk being detained or returned to abusive relatives, according to the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, or UNAMA.

Reliable nationwide figures are difficult to obtain because monitoring has become increasingly dangerous and many cases go unreported. But UN agencies have long estimated that nearly **9 in 10 Afghan women experience at least one form of physical, sexual or psychological violence during their lifetime**.

The crisis extends beyond abuse in the home. Since returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban have barred girls from education beyond the sixth grade and prohibited most women from working for nongovernmental organizations and the United Nations.

UNESCO said in 2024 that at least **1.4 million girls had been deliberately denied secondary education** since the Taliban takeover. Including girls who were already out of school, nearly **2.5 million — about 80% of school-age Afghan girls — were not attending classes**.

Women’s rights advocates say the restrictions have intensified isolation, forced marriage, economic dependence and mental-health problems.

“The Taliban have created the world’s most serious women’s rights crisis,” Heather Barr, associate women’s rights director at Human Rights Watch, has said, describing the policies as a systematic assault on women’s freedom and autonomy.

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Malala Yousafzai has also condemned the Taliban’s treatment of Afghan women and girls. “The Taliban do not see women as human beings,” she said at a 2025 summit on girls’ education, urging governments not to legitimize the group’s rule.

The UN has documented a sharp decline in women’s ability to influence decisions affecting their lives. In consultations cited by UN Women, almost all Afghan women surveyed said they had little or no influence in their communities. The agency has also reported signs of severe psychological distress, including women knowing of friends or relatives who had attempted suicide since the Taliban takeover.

The Taliban reject accusations that they are abusing women’s rights, saying their policies follow their interpretation of Islamic law and Afghan culture. They have repeatedly said girls’ secondary schools will reopen once unspecified conditions are met, but no national reopening has taken place.

Rights groups argue that the Taliban’s “morality” rules — enforced through arrests, intimidation and public punishment — constitute another form of state violence. Women have been detained over alleged dress-code violations, while protesters demanding education and employment have reported beatings, threats and imprisonment.

UN officials are calling for international pressure on Taliban authorities to restore women’s access to education and employment, reopen protection services and ensure survivors can report abuse without fear of retaliation.

Advocates say humanitarian aid remains essential but cannot substitute for rights.

“Afghan women are not asking the world to save them,” activists have repeatedly told international forums. “They are asking the world not to abandon them.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the findings of the U.N. annual human rights report on Afghanistan, focusing on rape, child marriage, domestic violence, civilian casualties, and the government’s failure to protect women.
counterfactuals.output:
The U.N. report portrayed violence against Afghan women as widespread, underreported, and largely unpunished:

- **Rape:** Women and girls faced rape by relatives, local power holders, armed men, and officials. Victims were often stigmatized, pressured to withdraw complaints, or even prosecuted for “moral crimes,” while perpetrators frequently escaped punishment.
- **Child marriage:** Forced and underage marriages remained common, despite legal restrictions. Such marriages deprived girls of education and exposed them to sexual abuse, early pregnancy, and further violence.
- **Domestic violence:** Beatings, sexual abuse, forced confinement, and other mistreatment within families were pervasive. Many women had little practical access to shelters, courts, police protection, or safe alternatives.
- **Civilian casualties:** The armed conflict continued to kill and injure large numbers of civilians, including women and children. Anti-government forces caused most casualties, though operations by government and international forces also harmed civilians.
- **Government failure:** Although Afghanistan had laws intended to protect women, the report said enforcement was weak and inconsistent. Police, prosecutors, courts, and political leaders often ignored complaints, favored informal settlements, or treated victims as offenders—creating a climate of impunity and leaving women without meaningful protection.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news report dated around 2009 on deteriorating conditions for Afghan women after the fall of the Taliban, citing Navi Pillay, Suraya Pakzad, and Wazhma Frogh.
counterfactuals.output:
**Afghan women face renewed insecurity eight years after Taliban’s fall**

*By Staff Correspondent*  
**KABUL, Nov. 25, 2009**

Eight years after the overthrow of the Taliban raised hopes of a new era for Afghanistan’s women, activists and United Nations officials say insecurity, weak government institutions and deeply entrenched discrimination are eroding many of the gains made since 2001.

Women have returned to schools, universities, government offices and parliament, and Afghanistan’s constitution formally guarantees equal rights. But outside the most protected parts of Kabul, many women still face forced marriage, domestic abuse, sexual violence and punishment for attempting to escape abusive families. Female teachers, aid workers, police officers and politicians have also been threatened or killed.

Navi Pillay, the United Nations high commissioner for human rights, has warned that violence against Afghan women remains widespread and is reinforced by a culture of impunity. Although Afghanistan has adopted legal and constitutional protections, she has said, those commitments are often not enforced by police, prosecutors or courts.

A 2009 report by the U.N. Assistance Mission in Afghanistan and the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights described violence against women as pervasive and largely hidden. It found that rape, “honour” killings, child marriage, forced marriage and domestic abuse were frequently treated as private family matters rather than crimes.

Pillay said the exclusion of women from decisions affecting Afghanistan’s future—including negotiations over security and possible reconciliation with insurgents—risked sacrificing their rights for political expediency. Women’s participation, U.N. officials argue, is essential if any peace settlement is to be durable.

### Shelters under pressure

For Suraya Pakzad, the founder of the Afghan group Voice of Women, the crisis is visible in the shelters her organization operates for women fleeing violence.

Pakzad began working clandestinely under the Taliban, organizing home-based classes for girls barred from school. Since 2001, her organization has expanded its work to include legal aid, literacy programs, counselling and refuge for women escaping forced marriages and abusive households.

Yet running shelters remains dangerous. Families sometimes accuse refuge workers of dishonouring them by protecting women who have left home. Conservative officials and religious leaders have also portrayed shelters as foreign institutions that encourage women to disobey male relatives.

Pakzad has said that many of the women arriving at shelters have nowhere else to go. Some have been beaten, traded to settle disputes or forced to marry at a young age. Others fear being killed if they return to their families. Even women who reach safety may remain in shelters for months or years because courts are slow, jobs are scarce and independent living is often socially unacceptable.

In western Afghanistan, aid workers have reported cases of women setting themselves on fire after prolonged abuse. Activists say self-immolation is often the desperate act of women who see no legal, economic or social means of escape.

### Law and reality

The government of President Hamid Karzai has pointed to women’s representation in parliament, rising school enrollment and the appointment of women to public positions as evidence of progress. Millions of girls have entered classrooms since the Taliban’s fall, and women now work as journalists, doctors, lawyers and civil servants.

But those achievements are uneven and fragile.

In rural areas, customary councils frequently decide cases involving marriage, rape and family disputes. Women and girls may be given in marriage to settle debts or blood feuds, a practice known as *baad*. Victims of rape can themselves be accused of adultery or “moral crimes,” particularly when police and judges fail to distinguish between consensual relations and sexual assault.

Wazhma Frogh, a women’s rights advocate associated with the Afghan Women’s Network, has argued that the country’s legal framework means little without enforcement. She has repeatedly called for women to have a meaningful role in drafting laws, overseeing government policy and shaping any negotiations with the Taliban.

Frogh and other campaigners were especially alarmed by the Shiite Personal Status Law, passed in 2009. An earlier version contained provisions widely criticized as allowing husbands to restrict their wives’ movement and as effectively sanctioning marital rape by tying maintenance to sexual submission. Karzai ordered revisions after protests at home and abroad, but women’s groups said the amended law still contained discriminatory provisions.

The controversy reinforced suspicions among activists that women’s rights could be bargained away to satisfy conservative political factions.

### Threats against public women

Women who enter public life face particular danger. Female officials and police officers have been assassinated, while girls’ schools have been burned or threatened in insecure provinces. Acid attacks on schoolgirls in Kandahar in 2008 sent a stark warning to families considering whether to educate their daughters.

In areas where the Taliban and other insurgent groups have regained influence, threatening letters and night-time warnings have forced some schools to close. Elsewhere, families keep daughters at home because of fighting, long distances to school, a lack of female teachers or fear of kidnapping and harassment.

The deterioration in security has also reduced the ability of aid organizations to monitor abuse. Female staff often cannot travel without male relatives or armed protection, and some districts have become inaccessible to government officials.

Activists say the danger does not come only from insurgents. Powerful commanders, local officials and family members are also responsible for abuse, while victims have little confidence that complaints will be investigated.

### Fear of political compromise

As Washington and its allies debate troop increases and ways to end the war, Afghan women’s groups fear that international fatigue could weaken support for their rights. Proposals to engage “moderate” Taliban members have intensified those concerns.

Pillay, Pakzad and Frogh have each emphasized, in different forums, that women must not be excluded from peace-building. Activists say reconciliation should require acceptance of the constitution and basic human rights, including women’s access to education, work, political participation and justice.

The Taliban’s removal in 2001 ended formal decrees that had barred most women from employment and girls from education. But campaigners caution that the fall of the regime did not eliminate the social structures, armed groups or conservative attitudes that sustained those restrictions.

For many Afghan women, progress since 2001 is real: a girl can attend school, a woman can vote, and female members of parliament can challenge government policy. Yet these gains coexist with violence inside the home, intimidation in public and a justice system that often punishes women for trying to protect themselves.

“The issue is no longer simply whether rights exist on paper,” one Kabul-based advocate said. “It is whether a woman can claim those rights without risking her life.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how worsening security in Afghanistan affects women and girls, using examples such as child rape, honor killings, forced marriage, restrictions on education and work, and attacks on women in public life.
counterfactuals.output:
Worsening security in Afghanistan affects women and girls through violence, displacement, weakened institutions, impunity, and increasingly restrictive Taliban policies. Although many abuses existed before the Taliban’s return to power in August 2021, conflict and the collapse of legal protections have intensified the risks.

- **Child rape and sexual violence:** Armed conflict, displacement, poverty, and weak law enforcement make children more vulnerable to rape and exploitation. Survivors may be blamed, threatened, forced to remain silent, or even punished for alleged “moral” offenses, while perpetrators often face little accountability.

- **“Honor” killings:** Families or communities may kill women and girls accused of relationships, refusing a marriage, or violating expected conduct. In insecure areas, courts, shelters, police units, and support services are limited or absent, allowing such crimes to be treated as private family matters rather than prosecuted.

- **Forced and child marriage:** Economic desperation and fear of violence can lead families to marry girls early, sometimes to settle debts or disputes or because they believe marriage offers protection. Displacement and the lack of schooling increase this pressure. Early marriage often exposes girls to domestic violence, early pregnancy, and lifelong dependence.

- **Restrictions on education and work:** Since 2021, Taliban authorities have barred most girls from secondary school and university and severely limited women’s employment. These measures reduce women’s income and independence, worsen shortages in sectors such as health and education, and make girls more vulnerable to early marriage and exploitation.

- **Attacks on women in public life:** Female officials, journalists, activists, judges, teachers, health workers, and police officers have faced threats, detention, assault, and assassination. Fear drives many into hiding or exile and removes women’s voices from government, media, justice, and peacebuilding.

These harms reinforce one another: insecurity closes schools and services; exclusion increases poverty and dependence; and the disappearance of women from public institutions further weakens protection and accountability. Women in rural areas, displaced families, ethnic and religious minorities, women with disabilities, and female-headed households often face the greatest risks.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a wire-service article with the dateline “UNITED NATIONS (CNN)” about reports that girls as young as seven are being raped in Afghanistan and that women’s rights remain poorly protected despite constitutional guarantees.
counterfactuals.output:
**UNITED NATIONS (CNN)** — Girls as young as seven have been raped in Afghanistan, according to reports cited by human rights advocates, highlighting the persistent dangers facing women and children despite constitutional guarantees of equal rights.

Activists and international officials say sexual violence, forced marriage and other abuses remain widely underreported, particularly in rural areas where victims may have little access to police, courts or medical care. Families often face intense pressure to remain silent because of stigma, fear of retaliation and concern that victims themselves could be punished or ostracized.

Afghanistan’s constitution formally recognizes equal rights for men and women. But rights monitors say those protections are frequently undermined by weak law enforcement, insecurity, corruption and the influence of conservative customary practices.

Women and girls who report rape can face further abuse within the justice system, advocates say. In some cases, authorities have treated victims as offenders, accusing them of adultery or running away from home. Shelters and legal-aid organizations remain limited and have faced political and social opposition.

The reports involving very young girls have intensified calls for Afghan authorities and the international community to strengthen investigations, prosecute perpetrators and expand services for survivors. Rights groups say those services should include confidential medical treatment, trauma counseling, safe housing and legal representation.

International officials have repeatedly warned that constitutional language alone cannot protect women and children without functioning institutions capable of enforcing the law. They have urged authorities to ensure that allegations of sexual violence are investigated promptly and that victims are not detained, coerced into settlements or forced to marry their attackers.

Reliable nationwide figures are difficult to obtain because many cases are never reported. Conflict, displacement and poverty also make it harder for monitors to document abuses or reach survivors.

Women’s rights advocates say lasting improvements will require more than criminal prosecutions. They are calling for trained female police officers, specialized courts, better child-protection systems and public education aimed at reducing the stigma surrounding sexual assault.

For many Afghan women and girls, campaigners say, the gap between rights promised on paper and protection in daily life remains dangerously wide.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
